causalMechanism.primaryVector: Bile-composition and gallbladder-motility sequence: in service-connected cirrhosis of the liver, three convergent derangements shift bile from cholesterol-saturated toward pigment-stone lithogenicity. First, hepatocyte dysfunction reduces bile-salt synthesis and canalicular bile-salt secretion, lowering the bile-salt pool and with it the capacity to keep cholesterol and unconjugated bilirubin in micellar solution. Second, portal hypertension with hypersplenism accelerates erythrocyte sequestration and turnover, while impaired hepatic glucuronidation reduces conjugation of bilirubin, so the biliary load of unconjugated, water-insoluble pigment rises. Third, gallbladder motor function is impaired in cirrhosis — reduced cholecystokinin responsiveness, gallbladder wall thickening, and elevated circulating estrogens from reduced hepatic clearance all promote stasis and crystal nucleation; the resulting stones in cirrhosis are most often pigment stones and are frequently asymptomatic. Del Olmo et al. (PMID 9361181), a controlled cohort of 313 histologically or laparoscopically confirmed cirrhosis patients against 357 liver-disease-free comparison patients, reported higher prevalence and incidence of gallstone disease in cirrhosis and concluded that cirrhosis of the liver may be considered a risk factor for cholecystolithiasis. Mallick and Anand (PMID 35535063) review the pathogenesis and management of gallstone disease in cirrhosis, reporting a prevalence of gallstone disease in cirrhosis of roughly 25 to 30 percent, substantially above general-population estimates, and attributing it to the altered bile composition and gallbladder dysmotility described above. Wang et al. (PMID 38382725), a systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 115 studies and more than 32 million participants, place pooled global gallstone prevalence at approximately 6.1 percent, which supplies the population-level comparator against which the cirrhosis-specific prevalence is contrasted. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected cirrhosis is asserted to have produced a new pathological entity, symptomatic chronic cholelithiasis, rather than merely to have worsened a baseline lithogenic tendency. A § 3.310(b) aggravation theory is not the theory offered here, because the literature describes stone formation in a previously stone-free biliary tree rather than measurable worsening of documented pre-existing stones; if the record shows gallstones documented before the cirrhosis-associated derangement, the case must be re-pleaded as aggravation of a baseline condition in which the cirrhosis-attributable increment is separated from the natural progression of age- and obesity-related stone disease, and § 3.310(b) then governs. Chronology is decisive: the corresponding § 3.310(a) and § 3.310(b) analysis requires imaging evidence of cholecystolithiasis after the clinical onset of cirrhosis, together with the cirrhosis diagnosis itself, so that the nexus opinion can state that the gallstone disease is at least as likely as not causally related to the service-connected cirrhosis — a conclusion that requires documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence, consistent with § 3.102 and with the requirement that the opinion rest on evidence of record rather than on speculation. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include advancing age, female sex, obesity and metabolic syndrome, rapid weight loss or bariatric surgery, pregnancy, hemolytic disorders independent of portal hypertension, hepatitis C infection and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease as separate hepatic drivers within the same liver, ileal disease or resection, prolonged fasting or total parenteral nutrition, and fibrate or somatostatin-analog medication, as well as genetic lithogenic predisposition; none of these operates to defeat the theory, but each must be addressed in the individual case because population-level relative risks do not transfer to the individual claimant. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating caution under § 4.14: cholelithiasis symptoms may be rated only once, and where the same abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting supports an evaluation of the cirrhosis or of a residual gastropathy, the rating schedule's own anti-pyramiding instruction for DCs 7301 through 7329 requires a single evaluation under the diagnostic code reflecting the predominant disability picture, so § 4.14 bars duplicative compensation for the same manifestations.

Primary condition: Service-connected cirrhosis of the liver (hepatic cirrhosis) with documented hepatic synthetic dysfunction or portal hypertension
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7312 (cirrhosis of the liver), assigned on Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score or on continuous daily debilitating symptoms with ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal hemorrhage, coagulopathy, portal gastropathy, or hepatopulmonary/hepatorenal syndrome, with Note (3) allowing rating on symptomatology where no Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score exists in the record
Secondary condition: Cholelithiasis (chronic gallstone disease, predominantly pigment stones) complicating service-connected cirrhosis of the liver
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7315 (cholelithiasis, chronic) — evaluated by reference to DC 7314 (chronic biliary tract disease): 30 percent with three or more clinically documented attacks of right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting in the past 12 months or requiring biliary stricture dilatation at least once in the past 12 months; 10 percent with one or two such documented attacks; 0 percent if asymptomatic with no documented attack in the past 12 months. Qualified-human rating review required; where stones are asymptomatic the schedule yields 0 percent, and where cholecystectomy complications dominate, DC 7318 applies instead
Original nexus theory: Causation

Legal boundary: § 3.310(a) concerns proximate causation; § 3.310(b) concerns attributable worsening beyond natural progression against a qualifying baseline. The at least as likely as not standard requires individual evidence and competing causes to be weighed. Apply claim-period rating criteria and § 4.14 nonpyramiding.
